title: Onesimus
lead: A slave of Philemon's household at Colossae who came to faith through Paul in prison and was sent home with the letter to Philemon and with Tychicus (Philemon 1:10-16; Colossians 4:9). His name means "useful," and Paul plays on it. Some decades later a bishop of Ephesus bore the same name; whether he was the same man is debated.

sections.b: Paul calls Onesimus "my own child, whom I fathered in my chains" (Philemon 1:10), and plays on his name: "Once he was useless to you. Now he is useful" (Philemon 1:11). He asks Philemon to have him back "no longer as a slave, but as more than a slave: a much-loved brother" (Philemon 1:16). Colossians 4:9 sends him home as "the faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you."

Ignatius of Antioch, writing to the church of Ephesus early in the 100s, praises their bishop Onesimus, "a man of inexpressible love." John Knox argued that this was Philemon's Onesimus, and that he helped collect Paul's letters. Lightfoot thought it possible but unlikely, since the name was common among slaves and Ignatius seems to speak of a younger man.
